content: International drug control encompasses global efforts to suppress the production, distribution, and consumption of illicit drugs. Several treaties that were once pivotal in international drug control are no longer in effect. These include: The International Opium Convention, which was signed in The Hague on January 23, 1912. The Agreement concerning the Manufacture of, Internal Trade in, and Use of Prepared Opium, signed in Geneva on February 11, 1925. The International Opium Convention, signed in Geneva on February 19, 1925. The Convention for Limiting the Manufacture and Regulating the Distribution of Narcotic Drugs, signed in Geneva on July 13, 1931. The Agreement for the Control of Opium Smoking in the Far East, signed in Bangkok on November 27, 1931. Currently, three major international treaties form the backbone of global drug control efforts: The 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, which establishes a framework for the control of narcotic substances. The 1988 United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, which focuses on combating drug trafficking and related criminal activities. Key international organizations involved in drug control include: The Commission on Narcotic Drugs, which serves as the central policymaking body for drug-related matters. The International Narcotics Control Board, which monitors the implementation of international drug control treaties. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, which provides support to member states in addressing drug-related challenges. For further reference, consult the UN International Drug Control Conventions, as provided by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, Regional Center for East Asia and the Pacific.
